newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia says no compromise on car policy.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says no compromise on car policy.

text.p: Indonesia said on Tuesday it does not intend to make any compromises over its controversial car policy in its bilateral talks with Japan, the European Union EU) and the United States.
"We don't see it that way," Trade and Industry Minister Tunky Ariwibowo told Reuters when asked if Indonesia is ready to make any compromises on its national car policy.
"But we are going to discuss (it). This is a good opportunity, everybody is here now," Ariwibowo said.
He said the national car policy would remain a major policy for the country. "We want to be independent in developing our industry which we consider to be strategic for our economy," he said.
The informal talks between Japan the EU and the United States would be held on the sidelines of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting in Singapore, he said.
The national car policy gives tax and tariff breaks to a car company controlled by President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra.

Earlier on Tuesday, Terence Johnsson, sales director of General Motors Corp unit PT General Motors Buana Indonesia (GMBI), said the car policy had hurt GM's sales and also affected future investment plans in Indonesia.
"The national car policy has created uncertainty in the market, which has affected our sales," Johnsson told Reuters in Jakarta.
Johnsson said GMBI was putting off planned capital injections because of the car policy but did not give details.
He said sales in 1996 were expected to touch 4,000 units, around 2,000 cars less than earlier projections. The GMBI plant in Indonesia began operations in January this year.
He said GMBI's flagship Opel Balzer, a five-door multi-purpose, 2,200 cc vehicle that uses 40 percent local parts, was expected to account for 3,200 of total sales.
PT Timor, Hutomo's joint-venture with South Korea's Kia Motors, was given special tax and tariff breaks by the government in January to produce the Timor sedan as the national car.
Under the deal, the Timor car must use 60 percent local content within three years of starting production, but currently it was importing fully assembled cars from South Korea.
Japan, the U.S. and the EU are fighting the policy at the WTO, arguing that it contravenes free trade regulations.
Ariwibowo said it is the right of GMBI to review their investment plans. "But I think the sales reduction is not only affecting General Motors," he said.
"Perhaps it (the reduction in sales) is also due to the slump in demand in Indonesia. It's something to do with consumer credit difficulties or difficulties in financing cars (purchases)."
Ariwibowo said the automobile industry is only one of many in the investment sector which is important to the Indonesian economy.

"We have so many other sectors that is attracting foreign investments," he said. "The investment incentives are quite adequate for Indonesia and it's reflected in the number of investment approvals which are very high especially during 1994 to 1996. In 1994, it's almost three times that of 1993."
